conceptTag: Building to last vs building to sell
readerTitle: Two plumbers, same size. One plans to stay, one plans to sell.
caseNote: 가상 사례 두 개 (배관 서비스 회사 두 곳, 소프트웨어 회사 두 곳). 모든 인물과 수치는 설명용
insight: 오래 갈 사업과 팔릴 사업은 '주인 없이 돌아가는 사업'이라는 핵심을 공유한다. 갈리는 지점은 시간, 돈, 약속이다. 가장 강한 위치는 팔 필요는 없지만 팔 수는 있는 사업이다.
misconception: 오래 운영할 사업이면 팔릴 준비는 신경 쓸 필요가 없다. 팔 사업이면 매각 직전까지 숫자만 좋게 만들면 된다.

sources.text: Warrillow, J. (2010). Built to Sell: Creating a Business That Can Thrive Without You. (주인 의존도를 줄이면 사업이 팔릴 수 있게 된다는 관점의 참고 자료)
모든 사례와 수치는 설명용 가상 예시

factChecks.note: 배관 회사 두 곳(Dan, Priya), 연 매출 약 $1.2M, 매도 계획 5년, 운영 계획 25년은 모두 설명용 가상 수치입니다.
송장 앱 사례의 '매출 35%', '개발자 절반'도 가상 수치입니다. 고객 집중이 사업 안정성과 매수자의 평가 모두에 불리하다는 일반 원리만 전달합니다.
'외부 투자자는 보통 언젠가 엑시트를 기대한다'는 벤처 투자의 일반적 구조에 대한 설명입니다. 모든 투자 형태에 해당하지는 않으므로 카드에는 'usually'로 적었습니다.
Warrillow(2010) 책의 출간 연도와 부제를 게시 전에 확인하세요. 카드 본문에는 책 내용을 인용하지 않았습니다.
장부 관련 문장은 특정 국가의 세무 조언이 아니라 '매수자가 믿을 수 있는 분리된 기록'이라는 일반 원칙만 다룹니다.

cards.title: Two plumbers, same size. One plans to stay, one plans to sell.
body: Dan and Priya each run a plumbing business in the same town. Each brings in about $1.2 million a year.
Dan plans to run his for 25 more years. Priya plans to sell hers in five.
Same trade, same size. But that one difference at the end quietly shapes almost every decision in between.

image.label: Two plumbing vans parked side by side, one with a calendar, one with a sale tag
image.brief: 같은 크기의 배관 서비스 밴 두 대가 나란히 서 있음. 왼쪽 밴 위에는 여러 해가 넘어가는 달력, 오른쪽 밴 위에는 작은 'For sale in 5 years' 꼬리표. 따뜻한 동네 거리 배경. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Priya wants a buyer in five years.
body: Priya has one year of profit to invest. Which change would matter most to a future buyer?

options.text: Cut prices to grow revenue fast, so the numbers look bigger
options.feedback: Revenue rises, but each job leaves less. A buyer will look at what the business keeps, not just what it bills.

options.text: Step out of daily jobs: hire a lead plumber, sell yearly maintenance plans, write down how jobs are priced
options.feedback: This costs her some profit now. In return, the business keeps running without her, and that is what a buyer is really paying for.

options.text: Buy new vans and a bigger office so the business looks established
options.feedback: Good equipment helps the work. But a buyer can buy vans anywhere. The question is whether customers and know-how stay after Priya leaves.

cards.title: Priya's changes make her business sturdier than Dan's.
body: Dan answers every call himself. He prices every job in his head and knows every customer by name. Customers love him.
But a business that runs on one person lasts only as long as that person can work. If Dan breaks his wrist, revenue stops. If he wants to retire early, there may be nothing to hand over.
Priya made her changes for a buyer. They also made her business more likely to last.

cards.title: Building to last vs building to sell
body: **Building to last** means designing a business you'll own for a long time, judged by the cash it produces year after year. **Building to sell** means designing it so someone else will pay for it, judged by what a buyer will see.
The two aims share a core: a business that runs without its owner. They split on three things: time, money and promises.

image.label: Two paths starting from one shared base, then splitting
image.brief: 인포그래픽. 아래쪽에 공통 기반 블록 'Runs without the owner'. 그 위에서 길이 두 갈래로 갈라짐. 왼쪽 'Build to last', 오른쪽 'Build to sell'. 갈림길 표지판에 'Time', 'Money', 'Promises'. 차분한 색, 로고 없음.

cards.title: Same tools, different trade-offs.
body: Once the business can run without its owner, the two goals pull in different directions.
list: **Spending:** a stayer can invest in things that pay back over ten years, like training apprentices. A seller favors what pays back before the sale.
**Growth:** buyers pay for the future, so sellers often push growth. Stayers can grow slower and keep more cash.
**Records:** a seller needs clean, separate books a stranger can trust. A stayer can get by with less, though it's risky.
**Promises:** a stayer can honestly tell staff "nothing will change." A seller can't.
cards.callout: Neither path is better. Each makes different trade-offs worth it.

cards.title: Two apps for dental clinics.
body: Two founders build booking software for dental clinics. The first raises money, spends ahead of revenue, and adds the features a large dental software company might want to buy. Her plan works if that buyer shows up at the right moment.
The second grows only on what customers pay. Growth is slower, but the business is profitable and she can keep it as long as she likes.
The first is a bet on one future moment. The second is a bet on many ordinary years.

image.label: Two growth lines: one steep and dashed toward a single point, one steady and solid
image.brief: 그래프 일러스트. 가파르게 오르는 점선이 'Exit?'라고 적힌 한 점을 향함. 그 아래로 완만하지만 꾸준히 오르는 실선이 길게 이어짐. 치과 의자 아이콘을 작게 배치. 실제 제품 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Both paths have a trap.
body: Building to sell can turn into dressing up: skipping repairs or training to make profit look higher before a sale. A careful buyer usually finds it. And if no buyer comes, you own a weaker business shaped for someone else.

Building to last can quietly become building around yourself. Plans change. Health, family or burnout can force a sale nobody prepared for, and a business that depends on its owner is hard to sell in a hurry.

cards.title: Now it's an invoicing app.
body: You run a small, profitable invoicing tool for freelancers. You'd like to keep it for years, but you're not sure.
A large agency wants a custom version. It would bring in 35% of your revenue and take half your developers. What do you do?

options.text: Take the deal. More revenue helps whether you stay or sell
options.feedback: You gain revenue but tie a third of it to one client who can leave. That weakens the business for you and for any buyer.

options.text: Decline, and spend the year making the product run without you: written support guides, a second developer who knows the code, more monthly plans
options.feedback: You give up quick revenue. In return, you get a business that can last and could be sold, so you keep both options open.

options.text: Raise outside money and grow fast so a bigger company notices you
options.feedback: It can work, but it quietly decides for you. Outside investors usually expect an exit, so you've chosen to build to sell.

cards.title: Build a business that could be sold, even if you never sell it.
body: A business that runs without you lasts longer and sells more easily. Then choose your trade-offs on time, money and promises on purpose.
**Try it today:** write down three things that would stop if you disappeared for a month. Pick one and start handing it off.
